Introduction:
Congenital anomalies (CAs), also known as congenital malformations or birth defects, are structural or functional anomalies that occur in utero . They may be identifiable prenatally, at birth, during infancy, or later in life. Globally, an estimated 240 000 newborns die annually within 28 days of birth due to congenital disorders, and 170 000 additional related deaths occur up to 5 years of age [ 1 ].

In recent decades, deaths from communicable diseases in both high- and low-income countries have decreased [ 2 ]. Consequently, the relative contribution of CAs to under-five mortality is now among the 10 leading causes of death worldwide [ 3 , 4 ].

For many CAs, including rare structural anomalies, most deaths occur in the first weeks of life, and survival beyond 10 years, conditional on surviving this crucial window, is actually quite high, frequently over 90% [ 5 ]. Children with cardiovascular, renal, and gastrointestinal abnormalities require specialized care. However, there is little population-based research about the long-term survival of individuals with a broad range of CAs beyond the second decade of life [ 3 ]. Information about the long-term outcomes of individuals with CAs who reach adulthood is important for counselling affected individuals and their parents and for adequate planning of health and other services [ 3 ].

We aimed to investigate associations between CAs and premature adult mortality. We focused on individuals who survived to the age of 18 years, comparing all-cause adult mortality of individuals with and without CAs in the Jerusalem Perinatal Study (JPS), a birth cohort with over four decades of follow-up. Previous work from this cohort had demonstrated a relatively high rate of CAs and an association between consanguinity and CAs [ 6 , 7 ].
Methods:
### Study design and study population

The population-based JPS cohort has been previously described [ 8 ]. It includes all 92 408 still- and live births to West Jerusalem mothers in 1964–76. Vital status was verified via linkage of unique national identity numbers to the Israeli Population Registry, updated through 31 December 2016. Data on demographic, perinatal, and parental characteristics were obtained at birth. We excluded stillbirths ( n = 949), offspring who could not be traced in the Population Registry ( n = 1409; henceforth “unverified”), and those who did not survive until 18 years of age ( n = 2429). The final study population consisted of 87 621 individuals ( Fig. 1 ).

### Study variables

The outcome variable was all-cause adult mortality, defined as deaths occurring at 18 years or older. Data on CAs and affected body systems were recorded postnatally using birth records, and updated during follow-up in the first months of life from hospitalization records, nurse examinations, and death certificates [ 6 ]. Prenatal ultrasound was not prevalent during this period. Starting in 1969 CAs were categorized in terms of severity according to the International Classification of Diseases (Seventh Edition), in use at the time [ 7 ]. Of 5538 individuals with missing CA status at birth, 5078 (92%) were defined as CA-free using data collected during postnatal follow-up ( Supplementary Methods ). However, the affected body system remained missing for 36% of infants with CAs.

We defined four exposures of interest: dichotomous CA status (none versus at least one), multiplicity (0 = none, 1 = single, and 2 = multiple anomalies), severity (0 = none, 1 = only mild/moderate anomaly, 2 = only severe anomaly, and 3 = moderate and severe anomalies combined). Finally, we assessed CAs in specific body systems, namely the cardiovascular, central nervous system (CNS), gastrointestinal, respiratory, genitourinary and musculoskeletal systems, ear or eye, other (unclassified), or “unknown” system. Risk of death was assessed separately by each system.

All multivariable models were adjusted for the following covariates: Offspring sex, birth weight in gram (<2500, 2500–4000, and >4000), mode of delivery (vaginal/caesarean section), maternal place of birth (Israel or abroad), maternal age at delivery (<20, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35+), maternal level of education at delivery (0–8, 9–12, and >12 years) and socioeconomic status recoded into three levels (low, medium, high) [ 8 ]. Participants with missing values for maternal age (0.7%), education (6.7%), and delivery mode (2.8%) were assigned a separate “missing” category and therefore retained in the multivariable analyses.

### Statistical analysis

We plotted crude survival probabilities from birth for the entire cohort by presence of CA and CAs in specific body systems ( n = 90 050), using the Kaplan–Meier approach and counting time from birth to death or end of follow-up (31 December 2016).

All subsequent analyses were based on the subsample of individuals who survived to 18 years of age ( n = 87 621). In multivariate models, time-to-event was defined from the 18th birthday to death or censored at the end of follow-up. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated by fitting Cox proportional hazard models. We also present adjusted absolute risks (1 − survival probability) and risk differences for individuals with and without CAs.

Separate models were constructed using the following exposures: CA status, number of CAs, anomaly severity, compared to a reference category of no CAs. Additional models compared mortality risks by the presence of a CA in a specific body system to “No CAs” or CAs in other systems. The models were adjusted for covariates previously found to be related to CA or death [ 9 , 10 ] and those found to be associated with mortality in univariate Cox models (not shown).

We conducted several sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Materials ): first, we assessed the impact of excluding “unverified” individuals by predicting their absolute risks over time from the CA status-mortality model using their baseline characteristics. We next compared these with observed risks in verified individuals using the Kaplan–Meier approach. Next, to evaluate the potential bias due to missing CA data in a few specific birth hospitals, we excluded infants born in these hospitals and compared results with the main models.

Thirdly, we imputed missing values in maternal age, education, and delivery mode using the multiple imputations by chained equations with five imputation datasets (R package mice ) [ 11 ]. The missing-at-random assumption was tested and supported by strong associations between the probability of missingness in imputed variables and the observed predictors.

To verify that our findings were robust to the non-independence of sibling observations, we conducted analyses selecting a single random child per family . Finally, since our data on family background are limited, we performed a sibling fixed-effects analysis. This design compares the mortality of siblings with and without anomalies within the same family and thus controls for unmeasured shared factors, including genetic background and household environment, that might confound the observed association.

For all main Cox models, the proportional hazards assumption was examined using the test of scaled Schoenfeld’s residuals [ 12 ] (R package survival [ 13 ]). Subsequently, we stratified all the main models on offspring’s sex and maternal education, which were the only variables exhibiting time-dependency ( Supplementary Tables S16–S19h and Figs S5–S8h ). The analyses were performed in R software (version 4.2.2).
Results:
The final study population is shown in Fig. 1 . Of the 92 408 offspring in the JPS cohort, 91 459 (99%) were live births, of which 90 050 (97.5%) were verified in the Population Registry. Kaplan–Meier plots illustrate mortality over the life-course ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ) for this population; most infants with malformations in cardiovascular and CNSs died very soon after birth and well before reaching 18 years. Of the verified population, 87 621 (97.3%) individuals attained the age of 18 years (and are the focus of this report), of whom 5621 (6.4%) had some form of CA.

Follow-up time from the 18th birthday ranged from 0 to 35 years with a median of 27.5 years and totalled 2 428 002.5 person-years. Deaths occurred in 1454 individuals from age 18.0 to 52.6 years; of these, 143 (2.5%) were in individuals with and 1311 (1.6%) without CAs ( Fig. 1 ).

Individuals with anomalies who survived to age 18 years were more likely to be male, to have low or high birth weight, low socioeconomic status at birth, Israel-born mothers, and to be delivered by caesarean section compared to those without CAs. Maternal age and education level at the time of delivery were similar between the groups ( Table 1 ), as was paternal age (mean 32 years ±7 in both). Of 5228 mothers whose children had CAs, about 7% ( n = 365) had more than one affected child.

In a multivariable Cox model, having any CA was associated with a 53% increase in the risk of death (CI: 1.29–1.83, P < .001) after stratification by offspring sex and maternal education and adjusting for other covariates ( Table 2 ).

Similar increased risks were observed for participants with single malformations (HR = 1.51, CI: 1.27–1.81) compared to those with none ( Table 3 ). The presence of multiple anomalies was associated with an even higher mortality risk (HR = 1.99, CI: 0.99–3.99), although the CI crossed unity. The risk of adult mortality was doubled in persons with severe anomalies (HR = 2.21, CI: 1.75–2.77) and with combined moderate and severe CAs (HR = 2.19, CI: 1.09–4.40) compared with those without anomalies. There was, however, no association between having a moderate anomaly and adult mortality. Adjusted HRs were elevated for CAs in the cardiovascular (HR = 4.81, CI: 2.15–10.70), gastrointestinal (HR = 2.74, CI: 1.47–5.11), and genitourinary (HR = 1.51, CI: 1.07–2.14) systems and among individuals with a CA in an unknown system (HR = 1.42, CI: 1.09–1.86) compared to all the others.

The absolute risk of death varied over time, and after 30 years of follow-up was 2.4% (CI: 1.8%–3.0%) in those with CAs, but only 1.5% (CI: 1.2%–1.9%) in those without, resulting in a risk difference of 0.9 percentage points ( Supplementary Figs S2 and S3 and Table S4 ).

All analyses aimed to assess the robustness of our findings produced results consistent with the main models. Supplementary Fig. S4 shows that the predicted risks for unverified individuals were almost identical to those of the verified cohort members in both exposure groups, suggesting that their risk of death is similar. The imputation analysis confirmed that missingness in covariates was unlikely to affect our results ( Supplementary Tables S6–S8 ). Likewise, the analyses excluding offspring born in hospitals with 75% of the missing CA status also supported our main estimates ( Supplementary Tables S9 and S10 ). Additionally, selecting a single random child per family suggested that non-independence of observations did not bias the reported associations ( Supplementary Tables S11–S13 ).

Finally, the fixed-effect within-family models were also consistent with the main analysis: siblings with CA, with all other shared characteristics being equal, had a 1.6-fold higher risk of adult mortality (CI: 1.06–2.42, Supplementary Table S14 ), and system-specific assessments, where there were sufficient cases to assess these, were generally consistent with the original models ( Supplementary Table S15 ).
Discussion:
In this population-based cohort, we found an increased risk of premature all-cause mortality among individuals with CAs who survived until adulthood. Moreover, participants with severe anomalies had an over two-fold higher risk. Having an anomaly in the cardiovascular system was associated with a striking almost five-fold increased risk, while anomalies in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary systems were associated with an almost three-fold and 1.5-fold increased risk of premature death in adulthood, respectively.

The association between the presence of any form of CA and all-cause mortality in adulthood has been rarely reported. A review of 55 studies showed that overall, long-term survival in children born with CAs was much lower than in reference populations, in agreement with our findings [ 3 ]. Nine of the included studies analysed long-term survival among those with any CAs, while 46 others focused on subtypes of anomalies. Most studies reported 1–5-year follow-ups, with the longest one being 25 years from birth [ 14 ], while in our study, the median follow-up was 46 years from birth, or 27.5 years after reaching adulthood.

We found a higher risk of premature adult mortality in those with combined severe and moderate CA as well as multiple CAs, although we had limited power to assess the latter. Similarly, a European cohort study noted that the presence of multiple structural anomalies is an important predictor of reduced survival [ 10 ].

Multiple studies have assessed mortality in individuals with cardiovascular CAs. A Swedish study with 19 years of mean follow-up in adulthood showed a 3.2-fold mortality risk among those with congenital heart disease [ 15 ], while a study based on United States census data reported that among those surviving past their first birthday, 76% of deaths occurred after age 18 years [ 16 ]. A Finnish nationwide cohort study reported increased long-term mortality in patients with atrial septal defects [ 17 ], while a single-centre study in Holland showed comparable mortality to the general population in individuals who underwent atrial septal defect repair, with surveillance up to 50 years [ 18 ]. Regarding ventricular septal defects, Eckerström et al . reported 1.5- and 2.5-fold increases in mortality in individuals with and without surgical repair, respectively, when compared with those without CAs, underscoring an increased risk of death in patients with CA despite treatment [ 19 ]. Our data did not allow us to distinguish the type of cardiac anomaly or its treatment.

Several conceptual frameworks can help explain our findings. Since most anomalies result from genetic or acquired insults to the developing foetus, our findings are congruent with the concept of long-term consequences of intrauterine events [ 20 ]. Muller and colleagues, reporting morbidity and mortality in patients with congenital heart diseases after correction or palliation, conjectured that the increased risks of adulthood death could be related to the accumulated lifetime comorbidities and risk factors in those affected by cardiovascular CAs [ 21 ]. Moreover, cardiovascular lifestyle risk factors such as obesity and decreased physical activity may be more prevalent among those with CAs and may increase with age, thereby, combined with the structural CAs, heightening the risk of premature death [ 22 , 23 ].

We found a strong association between gastrointestinal anomalies and adult mortality, not previously reported, to our knowledge. A follow-up of a cohort of patients with anorectal, urological, and gynaecological system anomalies found long-term functional disturbances [ 24 ]. Although these anomalies may be corrected surgically, affected individuals may remain vulnerable to continuous morbidity leading to premature mortality.

Similarly, we found a positive association between genitourinary anomalies and adult mortality. Urinary system abnormalities and childhood kidney diseases may cause chronic kidney disease with severe consequences for premature mortality and cardiovascular morbidity [ 25 ], including a five-fold risk of end-stage kidney disease in young adults [ 26 ]. However, we are unaware of reports of association between genitourinary anomalies and all-cause mortality after age 18.

This paucity of data may be due to a perception that genitourinary and gastrointestinal CAs are “less lethal” compared with the life-threatening/immediate consequences of cardiovascular anomalies [ 27–29 ]. The latter enjoy sustained attention throughout the lifespan, and affected individuals are usually closely followed up by specialized clinics [ 30 ]. Nevertheless, gastrointestinal and genitourinary anomalies can also be debilitating, and our findings support recommendations for more research and careful follow-up in the transition between paediatric, adolescent, and adult clinical care [ 31 ]. Indeed, recommendations for life-long follow-up for individuals with anogenital malformations have recently been made by the eUROGEN group [ 32 ].

A key strength of our study is its population-based design with rich data collection at baseline [ 8 ] and long follow-up, compared to most published studies. The multi-generational nature of the JPS provided robust data on the parents’ sociodemographic characteristics, while the sample size provided sufficient power to assess most of the exposures. Although we lacked data on familial genetic and behavioural factors (e.g. consanguinity, maternal smoking, or medications) on all cohort members (which might have influenced the risk and consequences of CA), the family-based design of the JPS allowed comparison of the mortality of siblings with and without anomalies, thus controlling for unmeasured shared family factors. Loss-to-follow-up is also uncommon in this cohort because the identification number given to all Israelis enables highly accurate data linkage to population-based registries, and emigration was rare.

The study has several limitations. First, 1409 participants lacked outcome data. However, sensitivity analysis demonstrated that excluding them was unlikely to bias the estimated CA-mortality associations. Second, the ascertainment of CAs took place prior to the widespread use of prenatal ultrasound, and CAs may have been missed. This would misclassify affected individuals as CA-free, biasing towards the null hypothesis. Data collection proceeded in stages; we used data collected later in life to correct and complete the data recorded at birth. Nevertheless, CA data were missing for 5078 individuals (5.8%), and, as has been done in previous JPS-based studies [ 6 , 7 ], we chose to classify them as CA-free, a decision that might also have contributed to bias towards the null hypothesis. Moreover, our findings remained robust in analyses that excluded infants born in hospitals with incomplete ascertainment of CAs. The affected body system was unfortunately unknown for 36% of 5621 newborns with CAs. An early study from our team estimated that all major CAs were fully recorded, though some minor ones may be missing [ 6 ]. The current study was underpowered to assess associations between CNS and respiratory malformations and adult mortality. Additionally, some covariate data were missing, but individuals with missing covariates were retained in the models, thus minimizing selection bias or diluted power. Imputation of missing values yielded similar effect sizes.

The JPS cohort represents the population of West Jerusalem during the study years, and includes Israel-born parents and immigrants from over 60 countries, representing various degrees of religious affiliation and practice [ 6 ], and a fairly high rate of consanguinity, itself associated with CAs [ 7 ]. Arab citizens of Israel are under-represented due to the geographic boundaries of the cohort, and they have patterns of CA and consanguinity patterns different from those of the Jewish population [ 33 ]. Finally, regarding generalizability to other geographic settings, the prevalence of CA in the JPS is comparable to that documented from Nordic countries with intensive reporting [ 34 ].

In conclusion, both the presence and severity of CAs increase the risk of premature adult death. Our findings that gastrointestinal and genitourinary CAs are associated with adult mortality add to the known association with cardiovascular anomalies and call for increased surveillance in these individuals. Given improvements in neonatal care, cardiac surgery, and chronic disease management over recent decades, it is expected that survival past childhood in individuals with CA will improve. Thus, focused long-term follow-up care, risk factor management in adulthood, and early detection of potentially fatal complications and prevention of chronic diseases among affected individuals will become more pertinent. Our findings call for more research into the mechanisms by which CAs may cause premature adult mortality, including exploring interactions with postnatal risk factors, such as exposure to diagnostic radiation and medications, obesity, and restricted physical activity.
Ethics approval: The study was approved by the institutional review board (Helsinki committee) at Hadassah University Hospital (HMO0200-09). Since anonymized retrospective data were used, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived.
